Function (f:X→Y)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Foundations of mathematics Set theory
OurBigBook.com Words: 7k Articles: 102
A function f:X→Y assigns exactly one output in the specified codomain Y to each input in its domain of a function X. Its rule may be a formula, a finite table, or another unambiguous assignment. The outputs actually reached form its image of a function f(X)⊆Y. A codomain states where outputs are allowed; the image of a function records where they actually land. Oscar Levin's introduction makes this distinction explicit. [ref].
For example, f:R→R, f(x)=x2, has the entire real line as its domain of a function and codomain, but its image of a function is [0,∞). Both −2 and 2 give the output 4: several inputs sharing an output is permitted. Assigning two distinct outputs to one input is not permitted. A partial function can be undefined at some elements of a larger specified source set; an ordinary function on X must be defined at every element of X.
Three properties describe how a function uses its target. An injective function never sends distinct inputs to the same output. A surjective function reaches every member of its specified codomain. A bijection does both, pairing each source element with exactly one target element. These are different requirements, as finite arrow diagrams show.
The chosen codomain matters even when the formula does not change. The function x↦x2 from R to R is not surjective, whereas the same rule from R to [0,∞) is surjective. Both fail injectivity. Further restricting the domain of a function to [0,∞) makes it a bijection onto [0,∞), with square root as its inverse function.
Functions make transformations composable: if f:X→Y and g:Y→Z, their function composition is (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)). Identifying each intermediate codomain prevents attempting to feed an output into a rule that is not defined there. When a transformation is a bijection, an inverse function recovers the original input without ambiguity. This is useful whenever information must be transported or a calculation reversed.

Complex-valued function (f:X→C)

Words: 42
Function OurBigBook.com
A function taking values in the complex numbers can be written uniquely as f=u+iv with real-valued functions u,v. Its Lebesgue integral is defined by integrating these components when ∣f∣ is integrable. Multiplication by a complex exponential of modulus one leaves this integrability unchanged.

Empty function (∅)

Words: 41
Function OurBigBook.com
The empty function has empty domain and empty graph. For any specified codomain there is exactly one function from the empty set into it. This explains why a cardinal product over an empty index set is one, including the convention 00=1 in cardinal exponentiation.

Dependent variable (y=f(x))

Words: 28
Function OurBigBook.com
A variable whose value is specified as a function of other variables. In an ordinary differential equation, the unknown function y is the dependent variable, and its argument x is the independent variable.

Function extensionality (f=g⟺∀x∈A, f(x)=g(x))

Words: 53
Function OurBigBook.com
For two mathematical functions f,g:A→B with the same domain and codomain, equality is equivalent to equality of their values at every argument. In the set-theoretic representation, their graphs of functions then contain exactly the same ordered pairs. This permits a function identity to be proved by fixing an arbitrary argument and proving the resulting value equality.

Essential variable of a function

Words: 80
Function OurBigBook.com
A coordinate of a function on a finite Cartesian product is essential if changing that coordinate, with all the others fixed suitably, can change the output. A coordinate is inessential precisely when such a change never affects the output in any context. If only coordinate i is essential, changing the other coordinates one at a time proves that the output is g(xi​) for a nonconstant unary function g. This deterministic dependence definition is not by itself a probabilistic or experimental notion of causal inference.

Pointwise maximum ((f∨g)(x)=max{f(x),g(x)})

Words: 35
Function OurBigBook.com
The function taking the greater value at every common-domain point. For finitely many affine functions it is a convex function, by bounding each affine branch by the convex combination of the endpoint maximum values. This is the finite-affine case of pointwise maximum of convex functions.

Pointwise minimum ((f∧g)(x)=min{f(x),g(x)})

Words: 60
Function OurBigBook.com
The function taking the lesser value at every common-domain point. It forms the lower envelope of two graphs. For finitely many affine functions it is a concave function: each affine branch is at least the corresponding convex combination of the two endpoint minimum values, so taking the minimum preserves that lower bound. A maximizing mixed strategy in a two-player zero-sum game maximizes such a lower envelope of opposing pure-choice expected payoffs.

Scalar-valued function (f:X→F)

Words: 61
Function OurBigBook.com
A scalar-valued function is a function whose codomain is a field, typically the real numbers or complex numbers. Its output is a single scalar, while its input can belong to an arbitrary set. For example, the square of the norm of a vector is real-valued. In a relativistic application, being scalar-valued alone does not establish Lorentz invariance: the transformation of the input and of the complete quantity must also be specified.

Implicit function

Words: 95
Function OurBigBook.com
An implicit function is a function specified through a relation between its input and output, rather than an explicit output formula. Locally, an equation F(x,y)=0 may specify y=g(x) if one output y is selected for each input x in a suitable domain. Different branches can define different functions; the relation itself need not give a unique output globally. For example, x2+y2=1 gives the two branches y=±1−x2​ on −1<x<1.
The implicit function theorem gives sufficient conditions for a unique local differentiable branch, while implicit differentiation computes its derivative by the chain rule. If F is continuously differentiable and Fy​=0, that derivative is g′(x)=−Fx​/Fy​ along the branch.

For functions f and g taking values in the same field, their quotient of functions is defined by (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x) on the common domain of a function restricted to points where g(x)=0. Thus f(x)=1 and g(x)=x on the real line give a quotient of functions defined only for x=0.

Codomain (Y in f:X→Y)

Words: 37
Function OurBigBook.com
The codomain of a function is its specified target set. The image of a function is a subset of the codomain, and equals it precisely for a surjective function. Changing a codomain can change whether the same input-output rule is surjective, as the quadratic function examples under function show.

Self-map (f:X→X)

Words: 92 Articles: 2
Function OurBigBook.com
A self-map is a function whose domain of a function and codomain are the same set. It need not be a bijection: a constant function on a two-element set is a self-map that merges its inputs. Self-maps can always be composed with one another, and all self-maps of a specified set form its full transformation monoid.

Idempotent function (f∘f=f)

Words: 52 Articles: 1
Self-map OurBigBook.com
A self-map f:X→X is idempotent if its function composition with itself leaves it unchanged: f(f(x))=f(x) for every x. Equivalently, every element of its image of a function is a fixed point. For example, the function on {a,b,c} sending a to b, b to b, and c to c is idempotent. A second application makes no further change.

Function composition (∘)

Words: 219 Articles: 1
Function OurBigBook.com
For functions f:X→Y and g:Y→Z, their function composition is g∘f:X→Z, defined by (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)). The rightmost function is applied first. Matching the intermediate codomain and domain of a function makes the expression well-defined.
For self-maps of the real numbers, take f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=2x. Then (g∘f)(x)=2x+2, whereas (f∘g)(x)=2x+1. Thus function composition need not be commutative. It does have the associative property: both (h∘g)∘f and h∘(g∘f) evaluate to h(g(f(x))) whenever each intermediate codomain matches the next domain of a function. The identity function leaves composition unchanged, making self-maps particularly useful as a monoid of transformations.

Injectivity and surjectivity under composition

Words: 133
Function composition OurBigBook.com
For f:A→B and g:B→C, the following implications hold. If both are injective, equality of two composite images can be cancelled first through g and then through f, proving that g∘f is injective. Conversely, if g∘f is injective, equality under f implies equality under the composite, so f is injective. If g∘f is surjective, every c∈C is g(f(a)), so g is surjective.
There are two useful strengthened cancellation rules. If g∘f is injective and f is surjective, lift any b,b′∈B with g(b)=g(b′) to preimages under f; composite injectivity then proves b=b′. If g∘f is surjective and g is injective, apply composite surjectivity to g(b) and cancel g to find a preimage of every b. Neither strengthened conclusion follows from the composite property alone.

Germ (mathematics, [f]x​)

Words: 54
Function OurBigBook.com
A germ at a point is an equivalence class of functions defined on a neighbourhood of the point: two representatives are equivalent if they agree on some smaller neighbourhood. A germ of a holomorphic function requires its representatives to be holomorphic functions; smooth and continuous germs use their corresponding classes of functions. The germ retains local behavior while forgetting the representative's values farther from the point.

Nonnegative function (f(x)≥0)

Words: 39
Function OurBigBook.com
A real-valued function is nonnegative when all its values are at least zero. Products and nonnegative linear combinations of nonnegative functions remain nonnegative. A nonnegative partition of unity gives convex combinations, hence a convex-hull bound for a geometric basis.

Commuting functions (R∘S=S∘R)

Words: 59
Function OurBigBook.com
Two self-maps R,S:X→X commute when R∘S=S∘R. Induction then gives Rn∘S=S∘Rn and Rn∘Sm=Sm∘Rn for all nonnegative integers m,n. Sharing a fixed point or invariant set does not by itself imply commutation. For rational sphere maps of degrees at least two, commutation does imply equality of their Fatou sets and Julia sets, by the commuting rational maps of degree at least two have the same Julia set theorem.

Finite modification of the identity on the real line (∣{x:f(x)=x}∣<∞)

Words: 67
Function OurBigBook.com
A finite modification agrees with the identity map outside a finite exceptional set. Sorting that set gives a unique finite record of pairs (x,f(x)). Real-number pairing by separated digits encodes the record in (0,1), and placing length-n records in disjoint intervals (n,n+1) gives an injection from all finite modifications into the real line. Conversely, changing the value at one fixed point gives a real-parameter family, so the Cantor-Schröder-Bernstein theorem shows this family has continuum cardinality.

Pointwise periodic self-map (∀x ∃nx​≥1: fnx​(x)=x)

Words: 162 Articles: 1
Function OurBigBook.com
A pointwise periodic self-map returns each point to itself after a positive number of iterates which may depend on the point. It is a bijection: each finite cycle supplies predecessors; equality of two images can be undone by an iterate with an exponent one below a common multiple of the two periods. The set consequently decomposes into disjoint finite permutation cycles. Pointwise periodicity does not imply that one iterate is the identity on an infinite set.

Uniform period criterion for pointwise periodic maps (fN=id⟺all cycle lengths divide N)

Words: 88
Pointwise periodic self-map OurBigBook.com
A pointwise periodic self-map has a uniform positive period exactly when its finite cycle lengths are bounded. A uniform period is divisible by every length; conversely, bounded lengths divide the least common multiple of 1,…,M for some bound M. Arbitrarily many bounded-length cycles are allowed. Every such map on a finite set has a uniform period. On any infinite set containing a countably infinite subset, cycles of unbounded finite lengths and fixed points elsewhere give a counterexample. Thus, with the usual axiom of choice assumption, the sets on which every pointwise periodic self-map has a uniform period are exactly finite sets.

Set function OurBigBook.com
On nonempty subsets of a nonempty finite set V, take the maximum of the contained element weights. Setting f(∅)=minv∈V​w(v) extends this to a monotone set function and a submodular set function. More generally any value at the empty set at most every element weight works, because Δx​f(S)=max{0,w(x)−f(S)} satisfies diminishing returns.

Marginal increment of a set function (Δx​f(S)=f(S∪{x})−f(S))

Words: 48
Set function OurBigBook.com
The marginal increment measures how much a set function changes when one new element is added. Usually x∈/S is required; if x∈S, the displayed difference is zero. The marginal increments of a modular set function depend only on x. The marginal increments of a submodular set function can only decrease as the input subset grows without acquiring x.

Modular set function (h(A)+h(B)=h(A∪B)+h(A∩B))

Words: 86
Set function OurBigBook.com
On a finite ground set, a modular set function is a set function satisfying the displayed equality for every pair of subsets. Equivalently,
h(S)=c+∑x∈S​ax​,c=h(∅),ax​=h({x})−h(∅).
(1)
To prove this representation, apply the equality to disjoint S and {x}: h(S+x)−h(S)=h({x})−h(∅). Add these fixed marginal increments along any ordering of S. Conversely, the contributions of each element and of the constant cancel in the displayed identity. Thus a modular set function need not be a normalised set function; its normalised instances are precisely the real-valued set functions with finite additivity on a finite power set. Adding or subtracting a modular set function preserves submodularity.

Symmetric set function (f(S)=f(V∖S))

Words: 39
Set function OurBigBook.com
A set function on the power set of a ground set V is symmetric when complementary subsets have equal values. A hypergraph cut function has this property because swapping the two sides changes no crossing hyperedge. If a symmetric set function is also a monotone set function, it is constant: f(∅)≤f(S)≤f(V)=f(∅).

Monotone set function (A⊆B⇒f(A)≤f(B))

Words: 43
Set function OurBigBook.com
A real-valued set function is monotone, in the nondecreasing convention, when enlarging its input subset cannot decrease its value. Equivalently, each marginal increment Δx​f(S) is nonnegative. This follows by adding elements individually; the converse follows by considering S⊆S∪{x}. A normalised set function with this property is a nonnegative function.

Normalised set function (f(∅)=0)

Words: 22
Set function OurBigBook.com
A set function is normalised when its value at the empty set is zero. Subtracting the constant f(∅) normalises any real-valued set function and preserves submodularity and the monotone set function property.

Finite additivity of a set function (F(A∪B)=F(A)+F(B)(A∩B=∅))

Words: 59
Set function OurBigBook.com
A real-valued set function on an algebra of sets is finitely additive if it has the displayed property for disjoint pairs. It follows that F(∅)=0. On a finite ambient set, induction gives F(A)=∑x∈A​F({x}), so arbitrary signed singleton weights describe all such functions. Summing the pointwise indicator function identity for the inclusion-exclusion principle against these weights proves the same formula for F.

Supermodular set function (f(S∪T)+f(S∩T)≥f(S)+f(T))

Words: 44
Set function OurBigBook.com
A real-valued set function is supermodular if it satisfies the displayed inequality. Its negative is a submodular set function. Equivalently, the gain from adding an element cannot decrease as the set grows. This is the defining property of a convex cooperative game, and makes coalition marginal allocations lie in the core of a cooperative game.

Submodular set function (f(A)+f(B)≥f(A∪B)+f(A∩B))

Set function OurBigBook.com
A set function is submodular if f(A)+f(B)≥f(A∪B)+f(A∩B) for every pair of subsets. Entropy submodularity is a fundamental example.

Every real-valued submodular set function on a finite ground set V is the sum of a normalised set function g that is nonnegative, monotone and submodular, and a modular set function h. A useful explicit choice is
dx​=f(V)−f(V∖{x}),h(S)=f(∅)+∑x∈S​dx​,g=f−h.
(2)
Proof. The formula makes h a modular set function, so g is a submodular set function. It is a normalised set function because h(∅)=f(∅). For x∈/S, diminishing returns gives Δx​f(S)≥Δx​f(V∖{x})=dx​, hence Δx​g(S)≥0. Thus g is a monotone set function, and starting at zero makes it a nonnegative function. Exact-cover inequality for submodular set functions (∑i=1t​f(Ti​)≥kf(T))

Submodular set function OurBigBook.com
Suppose f is a normalised set function and a submodular set function, and T1​,…,Tt​⊆T cover every element of T exactly k times, counting repetitions in the indexed collection. Then the displayed inequality holds. Neither the monotone set function property nor the nonnegative function property is required.
Proof. Fix an ordering of T and write aj​=f(Pj​)−f(Pj−1​) for its successive marginal increments. The chain lower bound for a submodular set function gives f(Ti​)≥∑xj​∈Ti​​aj​. Summing counts each aj​ exactly k times, and ∑j​aj​=f(T). Exact coverage matters because the aj​ may be negative. For a monotone set function, the same argument also allows each element to occur at least k times.

Submodular set function OurBigBook.com

Then the displayed inequality holds for every U⊆T, with equality for U=T. The right side is a modular set function lying below f on the power set of T and touching it at the top.
Proof. Reveal the elements of U in the chosen order. Immediately before adding xj​∈U, the conditioning set is U∩Pj−1​⊆Pj−1​. Function collision (x=x′,f(x)=f(x′))

Words: 138
Function OurBigBook.com
A function collision is a pair of distinct inputs x=x′ with f(x)=f(x′). An injective function has no collisions. For a two-to-one function every nonempty fiber has two elements and hence one unordered collision pair. Finding such a pair through an oracle is the task of quantum collision finding.
In the finite example under image and preimage of a function, the pair {a,b} is a function collision: both inputs give zero. The function retains their shared output but loses the distinction between them. If a finite set has more inputs than the number of available outputs, the pigeonhole principle forces a function collision. Equal source and target cardinalities alone do not prevent one.
For a finite function, let my​ be the cardinality of its fiber of a function over y. The number of unordered function collisions is ∑y​(2my​​), because each pair must lie in one common fiber. The example's nonempty fiber sizes are 2,1,1, giving exactly one collision pair.

Fiber of a function (f−1(y))

Words: 420 Articles: 1
Function OurBigBook.com
For a function f:X→Y and y∈Y, its fiber of a function over y is the set of all inputs producing that one output:
f−1(y)=f−1({y})={x∈X:f(x)=y}.
(4)
Here f−1(y) is shorthand for a preimage of a singleton set, rather than a claim that an inverse function exists. A fiber can contain several inputs or be empty. It describes exactly which distinctions the function forgets.
For the finite function under image and preimage of a function, the fibers over 0,1,2,3 are {a,b}, {c}, {d} and the empty set, respectively. The nonempty fibers form a partition of a set: they are disjoint sets whose union is the domain of a function. Every input belongs to the fiber over its unique output, and two fibers with distinct output labels cannot share an input. A function is injective exactly when every fiber has at most one member; it is surjective exactly when every member of its specified codomain has a nonempty fiber.
More generally, f−1(U) is the union of the fibers over all y∈U. The relation x∼x′ defined by f(x)=f(x′) is an equivalence relation, and its equivalence classes are precisely the nonempty fibers. The resulting quotient set is naturally in bijection with the image of a function. This links an input partition to the output values actually reached, without choosing one representative from each class.
Fibers are useful when an output is known but the input is not uniquely determined. A solution set g−1({0}) is one fiber, and factorization through a surjection explains when another function depends only on the retained output. Quantum hidden subgroup problem algorithms use functions whose fibers are cosets, giving the same idea a structured form in group theory.

Factorization through a surjection (g=h∘f)

Words: 174
Fiber of a function OurBigBook.com
For a surjective function f:B→A and a function g:B→C, there is a unique function h:A→C with g=h∘f if and only if g is constant on each fiber of a function of f. Define h(a) to be the common value on f−1(a); it is well-defined and unique because that fiber is nonempty. This uniquely specified value requires no simultaneous arbitrary choices.
For a concrete example, restrict the codomain of the finite function above to its image of a function I={0,1,2}, making f:A→I surjective. Define g(a)=g(b)=5, g(c)=7 and g(d)=9. Then h(y)=2y+5 on I gives g=h∘f: knowing the output of f is enough to compute g. If instead g(a)=g(b), no such h can exist, because h(f(a))=h(f(b)) must be the same value.
The surjectivity assumption supplies uniqueness on the full target. If the original unused target value three were retained, the factorization would impose no condition on h(3), and different extensions could agree on every actual input. Thus factorization through a surjection formalizes when a compressed description retains all information needed for a later calculation.

Inverse function (f−1)

Words: 653 Articles: 6
Function OurBigBook.com
An inverse function reverses a bijection. For f:X→Y, it is a function g:Y→X satisfying
g∘f=idX​,f∘g=idY​.
(6)
Equivalently, g(f(x))=x for all x∈X and f(g(y))=y for all y∈Y. We write g=f−1. The superscript denotes reversal through function composition; it does not mean the pointwise multiplicative inverse 1/f(x). The preimage notation f−1(B) for a set B is also distinct: a preimage exists even when no inverse function exists.
For a computed example, let f:R→R be f(x)=2x+1. Solving y=2x+1 for x gives g(y)=(y−1)/2. Thus f(1)=3 and g(3)=1; direct substitution gives g(f(x))=x and f(g(y))=y throughout the real line. In contrast, 1/f(3)=1/7, which does not undo f(1)=3.
Why must f be a bijection? If f(x1​)=f(x2​), applying g gives x1​=x2​, proving injectivity. For any y∈Y, the equation f(g(y))=y supplies a source element, proving surjectivity. Conversely, a bijection supplies exactly one predecessor for each y, defining a unique inverse function. A left inverse or right inverse requires only one of the two composition identities.
For f(x)=x2 on the real line, the equation f(x)=4 has two solutions, x=±2, so its arrows cannot be reversed as one function on all inputs. The restriction to [0,∞) removes that ambiguity. As a bijection from [0,∞) onto [0,∞), it has inverse function g(y)=y​. The identity x2​=∣x∣ explains why x2​=x works on the restricted domain of a function but fails for negative x. [ref].
More generally, (a,b) lies on the graph of a function f precisely when (b,a) lies on the graph of a function of its inverse function. This coordinate swap explains the geometric reflection and the horizontal line test. It also explains why inverse sensitivity is reciprocal locally: the inverse function rule divides by the original derivative at the corresponding input, when that derivative is nonzero.

For a real-valued function drawn in the plane, the horizontal line test asks whether every horizontal line intersects its function graph at most once. This is exactly injectivity, since two intersections at the same height mean two inputs have the same output. A missing height is compatible with injectivity, so an inverse function is then defined on the image of a function; it is an inverse on the entire specified codomain only when surjectivity also holds.

The nonzero derivative condition also ensures local invertibility; it does not assert a global inverse function on an arbitrary larger domain of a function. At a=0, this division is unavailable: the nonnegative restriction still has a square root inverse, but its finite derivative at zero does not exist. [ref].

For a continuous function on a compact interval, interpolants along grids with mesh tending to zero converge in the uniform norm; their error is bounded by the modulus of continuity at the mesh size.

A linear interpolant is the unique polynomial of polynomial degree at most one taking prescribed values ya​,yb​ at distinct interpolation nodes a,b. It is an affine function, including the constant function case. For a≤x≤b, its two displayed coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one, so changing each sampled value by at most δ changes every interpolated value by at most δ. f(x)=cfor every x∈X.​

A constant function from the real line to the real numbers has derivative zero and every nonzero real period of a function; there is no smallest positive period. It supplies a reference level from which variation can be measured.
A constant map between vector spaces is a linear map only when its value is the zero vector, since a linear map must preserve zero. A nonzero constant map is still an affine map. In a Fourier series, the constant term records the period average, while the other terms describe oscillation around that level.

A real-valued function has codomain contained in the real numbers.

The positive part of a real-valued function f is f+​(x)=max(0,f(x)). Together with its negative part, it gives f=f+​−f−​ and ∣f∣=f+​+f−​.

Real-valued function OurBigBook.com
The negative part of a real-valued function f is the nonnegative function f−​(x)=max(0,−f(x)). It records the magnitude of the negative values, rather than retaining their sign: if f(x)=−3, then f−​(x)=3. Together with the positive part, it gives f=f+​−f−​ and ∣f∣=f+​+f−​. Function OurBigBook.com
A bijection f:X→Y is a function that is both injective and surjective: each element of its codomain is the output of exactly one element of its domain of a function. The two requirements exclude unused targets and merged inputs respectively. The finite example f(A)=1, f(B)=2, f(C)=3 is a bijection from {A,B,C} to {1,2,3}, whereas adding an unused target 4 makes that same rule fail surjectivity.
A bijection gives an inverse function by reversing every pairing. Conversely, a two-sided inverse function implies a bijection, as the proof under inverse function shows. This is useful for transporting structures without losing or identifying elements. It also defines equality of cardinality: two sets have equal cardinality exactly when a bijection pairs them. An infinite example is n↦2n from the integers to the even integers, with inverse m↦m/2 on that specified codomain. A proper subset can therefore have the same cardinality as an infinite set. [ref].

Periodic function (f(x+T)=f(x))

Words: 1k Articles: 13
Function OurBigBook.com
A periodic function repeats exactly after a nonzero shift of its input. For f:R→Y, a positive period of a function T satisfies
f(x+T)=f(x)for every x∈R.​
(9)
One interval of length T therefore determines the whole function. For another domain of a function D, a period must also preserve the domain, D+T=D; equality only where two domains happen to overlap is weaker. Periodicity is an exact translation of a function symmetry, rather than merely two similar-looking pieces of its graph.
The sine sin(2πx) has fundamental period one. The function sin2(2πx) repeats after half a unit: the sine changes sign under that shift, but squaring removes the sign. The mixed function g(x)=2+sin(2πx)+21​cos(4πx) again has fundamental period one. All positive integer multiples of a period are periods, so specifying one period need not identify the shortest repetition.
If the input is time and T0​ is the fundamental period, the frequency is 1/T0​ and the angular frequency is 2π/T0​. Repetition lets a Fourier series describe a cycle using sines and cosines; the period average separates the reference level from the oscillating terms. Strang develops this representation and its Fourier coefficients in §4.1 of Computational Science and Engineering by Gilbert Strang.[ref]
This connection grew out of a physical problem. In his 1822 book Théorie analytique de la chaleur by Joseph Fourier, Joseph Fourier used periodic functions to extend profiles beyond their initial interval while treating heat conduction. Chapter III, §§233–234 combines even functions and odd functions into sine–cosine expansions and rescales their period.[ref] A modern Fourier series interpretation still requires the appropriate convergence conditions.
A constant function has every real shift as a period and no fundamental period. Without continuity, even a nonconstant periodic function can lack a smallest positive period; periodic function without a least positive period gives a concrete example. The period group of a function organizes all these possibilities.

∫aa+P​f=∫rr+P​f=∫rP​f+∫PP+r​f=∫rP​f+∫0r​f=∫0P​f.
(10)
No differentiability is required. This also allows the Fourier coefficients of a periodic function to be computed on any interval of one full period.

Periodic function OurBigBook.com
Periodicity is invariance under translation by a nonzero period P: a periodic function satisfies f(x+P)=f(x) at every point in its domain, with translation preserving the domain. For an angular coordinate on a full circle, single valuedness requires 2π-periodicity. The sine and cosine factors sin(kθ) and cos(kθ) are 2π-periodic for nonzero real k precisely when k is an integer. Their Fourier series supply the angular modes for the harmonic expansion on a disk.

The resulting periodic function has period T. If the endpoint limits of f differ, the extension has a jump discontinuity at every period boundary. Under the usual piecewise-smooth convergence hypotheses, its Fourier series takes the average of the two one-sided limits there; an assigned value at an isolated endpoint does not change the Fourier coefficients.

Its periodic extension has distributional derivative −h, with no endpoint Dirac delta distribution.
